ethics_check.title: Ethics Approval Check
ethics_check.summary_text: All papers that appeared to involve live data collection contained an ethics approval statement.

table.text: The adult study was approved by the Ethics Committee of the Institute of Psychology at Humboldt-Universität zu Berlin (2022-65) and the child study by the Ethics Committee of the Institute of Psychology at the University of Greifswald (BB 166/23).

The study conducted with adults was approved by the Ethics Committee of the Institute of Psychology at Humboldt-Universität zu Berlin (reference number 2022-65) and the study conducted with children by the Ethics Committee of the Institute of Psychology at the University of Greifswald (reference number BB 166/23).
In the adult sample, seven participants were excluded (for details, see Woitow et al., 2026), resulting in a final sample of 79 adults (52 women; M = 23.80 years, SD = 4.12).
table.formatted: In the adult sample, seven participants were excluded (for details, see <ref type="bibr">Woitow et al., 2026)</ref>, resulting in a final sample of 79 adults (52 women; M = 23.80 years, SD = 4.12).

table.text: In the child sample, six participants were excluded due to an excessive number of missing responses in the learning and memory tasks (> 3 SDs above the group mean).
table.formatted: In the child sample, six participants were excluded due to an excessive number of missing responses in the learning and memory tasks (> 3 SDs above the group mean).

table.text: All participants had normal or corrected-to-normal vision, and children had no history of developmental disorders.
Written informed consent was obtained from adult participants and from children's parents, and children gave their assent before participation.

All participants completed the same experimental conditions in one session lasting approximately 70-80 minutes and were compensated with €10 per hour plus a bonus (€2 for adults, small gift for children).
Following the learning task, participants completed a surprise recognition memory test for images encountered during learning.
In both tasks, participants were instructed to collect as many points as possible and were told that the bonus depended on their performance.
To maximize points, participants had to learn the changing reward probabilities and adjust their choices accordingly.
To ensure attention, participants had to press the spacebar in OL trials to see the other player's choice.
Participants were introduced to the two image categories and shown example images for each.
Additionally, participants were advised to attend to trial values and images throughout the task.
At the end of the experiment, participants completed a questionnaire (Supporting Information: Debriefing questionnaire).
In the pilot, participants completed a learning task containing only 80 experiential learning trials.

ethics_check.report:

> In the child sample, six participants were excluded due to an excessive number of missing responses in the learning and memory tasks (> 3 SDs above the group mean).

> All participants had normal or corrected-to-normal vision, and children had no history of developmental disorders.

> Written informed consent was obtained from adult participants and from children's parents, and children gave their assent before participation.

> All participants completed the same experimental conditions in one session lasting approximately 70-80 minutes and were compensated with €10 per hour plus a bonus (€2 for adults, small gift for children).

> Following the learning task, participants completed a surprise recognition memory test for images encountered during learning.

> In both tasks, participants were instructed to collect as many points as possible and were told that the bonus depended on their performance.

> To maximize points, participants had to learn the changing reward probabilities and adjust their choices accordingly.

> To ensure attention, participants had to press the spacebar in OL trials to see the other player's choice.

> Participants were introduced to the two image categories and shown example images for each.

> Additionally, participants were advised to attend to trial values and images throughout the task.

> At the end of the experiment, participants completed a questionnaire (Supporting Information: Debriefing questionnaire).

> In the pilot, participants completed a learning task containing only 80 experiential learning trials.

Ethics approval statement:

> The adult study was approved by the Ethics Committee of the Institute of Psychology at Humboldt-Universität zu Berlin (2022-65) and the child study by the Ethics Committee of the Institute of Psychology at the University of Greifswald (BB 166/23).

power.title: Power Analysis Check
report:
::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

table.title: Effect of experiential and observational learning on memory across development
table.existing_data_explanation: No, no data have been collected for this study yet.
table.research_questions:
We will investigate whether experiential vs. observational learning affects recognition memory differently across development. Children (8-10 years) will perform a learning task followed by a surprise recognition memory test. 
The learning task consists of interleaved experiential and observational learning trials. At the beginning of a trial, participants will be informed if it's their turn (experiential learning) or if they observe another player (observational learning). Next, a value (potential reward) is shown followed by an image. During the image display, participants must decide whether they want to gamble (play) for the value or not (pass) (experiential learning) or observe another player's play-pass choice (observational learning). Next, the trial outcome (winning, losing, or neutral) is presented. The images are assigned to two categories (animate vs. inanimate) which reflect opposing reward probabilities that change throughout the task. After choosing play, participants are rewarded based on the reward probability. When passing, they see the hypothetical outcome. In observational trials, participants see the other player's feedback. 
In the following memory test participants see the images from the learning task interleaved with new but semantically matching images. For each image, they must state if it is old or new and rate their confidence. 
Based on previous developmental studies, we expect children to show better memory performance for images seen during experiential compared to observational learning trials. In adults, we could reveal enhanced memory for experienced and observed gambling (Woitow et al., work in progress). Whether this is similar in children will be explored. Overall, we expect children in both learning conditions to remember the images reliably (above-chance level). However, compared to adults we expect children to show reduced memory accuracy. Moreover, based on previous developmental studies, we expect developmental differences between children and adults in experiential and observational learning as well as gambling behavior.
We will investigate underlying computational mechanisms during experiential and observational learning. Here, we will examine how prediction errors (PE) during learning are linked to subsequent memory and whether this differs across development. Previous research in adults showed a positive effect of PEs during experiential learning on memory. However, no study to our knowledge examined this link in children. Overall, we expect differences between children and adults in PE coding and its effect on memory due to maturational changes in involved brain regions from childhood to adulthood.
table.design_dependent_variables:
Behavioral variables: (1) Learning task. For experiential learning trials, we will record the decision (play or pass) and the decision time (reaction time). In observational learning trials, participants must press the spacebar during image display to see the other player's choice. Here, we will record key press and reaction time. (2) Memory task. During the memory test, participants must state for each image whether it is old (seen in the learning task) or new (not seen before). Then, participants rate their confidence regarding their choice on a scale from 1 (guess) to 4 (completely certain). We will combine the two responses to one memory score ranging from 1 (new and highest confidence) to 8 (old and highest confidence) representing our key dependent variable to assess memory performance. 
Computational variables: (1) We will use a Bayesian ideal observer model to calculate the expected reward probability for each trial while considering changes in the reward probability (change points, CP) (see Jang et al., 2019 for further details). The model will be given information about the true probability of the CP occurrence for each trial (hazard rate). Based on the estimated reward probability we will calculate the trial-by-trial learning rate. (2) Following Jang et al. (2019), we will calculate PEs during the value, image, and feedback phase. The value PE depends on the possible values (1, 5, 10, 20, 100) shown during each trial. The image PE is computed by calculating the PE before and after the image display (see Jang et al., 2019 for further details). We assume the reward expectation before seeing the image category to be the average across both categories. The image PE is computed as the difference between reward expectation before and after observing the image category. The feedback PE depends on the possible outcomes of a trial (winning, losing, or neutral). (3) Further, we want to investigate the effect of other computational factors like surprise and uncertainty on recognition memory. Surprise (trial-by-trial changes of CP probability) will be computed by marginalizing over expected reward probabilities. Uncertainty will be measured by calculating the entropy of the posterior probability distribution of the reward probability for each trial.
table.study_design_overview: The study follows a within-subject design. Each participant will perform 160 learning trials (80 trials per learning condition, switch after 1-2 trials of the same condition) and 320 memory trials (interleaved 160 old and 160 new images). However, each participant performs a unique task since the reward probability can change on each trial with a probability of 0.16 to a random value between 0 and 1 (no CP during the first 20 trials of the learning task and first 15 trials after a CP occurred).
table.statistical_tests:
Our data analysis will follow the analysis from our previous study in adults (Woitow et al., work in progress) to enable comparison of results. Thus, we will use the predicted reward probability estimated by the Bayesian ideal observer model when including reward probability in the analyses. (1) Learning. To investigate the choice behavior during the learning task we will fit different reinforcement learning (RL) models to participants' choices. Our base model contains four parameters: (1) temperature parameter, (2) value exponent term (effect of trial value on choice behavior), (3) play bias term (tendency to attribute higher values to play decisions), and (4) learning rate. This base model will be compared to additional RL models which contain the same four parameters and additional ones (e.g. surprise, uncertainty). Besides, we will determine separate learning rates for experiential and observational learning. We will compute the Bayesian information criterion (BIC) for each model and compare them. The model with the lowest BIC will then be used to simulate choice behavior to compare participants' behavior to model-predicted behavior. (1) Memory. Memory accuracy will be first assessed by determining hit rates and false-alarm rates and comparing them between experiential and observational learning as well as between play and pass trials. To check if participants' memory performance was better than chance, we will apply a one-sample t-test to d-prime (hit rates - false-alarm rates) values. Further, we will examine if the subjective confidence rating reflects true memory strength by testing if memory accuracy is better for higher than lower confidence. Next, we will check whether memory scores (1 to 8) differ between experiential and observational learning and between play and pass trials. (3) Learning & Memory. The link between learning-related computational factors and memory will be examined for each participant and factor. We will check for the overall effect of these factors on memory scores and compare them between learning conditions and between play and pass trials. Besides, we will model participants' memory scores using a hierarchical regression model to examine the contribution of learning-related computational factors to subsequent memory performance. 
We will compare results in children to results in adults from our previous study (Woitow et al., work in progress) and combine data from both studies for joint analyses to investigate developmental differences.
table.outliers_and_exclusions: The criteria for excluding observations and participants are based on our previous study (Woitow et al., work in progress) (1) Learning task. We will exclude participants who do not show an above-chance performance during the learning task. To determine the above-chance performance we will simulate random choices using the same learning task structure and compute the total score achieved. We will repeat this simulation 5.000 times and then assess whether the participant's score is bigger than 5% of the score distribution from the simulations. (2) Learning & Memory task. We will remove experiential learning trials, and old-new choice trials from the memory task in which participants responded faster than 200ms. Subjects will be removed when they have too many fast response trials (> 3 std from the group mean). Further participants will be removed if they do not respond in too many trials (> 3 std from the group mean).
table.sample_size: Our sample size will be 80 participants (N = 80). The number of participants is based on the sample size of our previous study in adults (Woitow et al., work in progress) to allow comparison of results.
table.additional_comments: In a post-questionnaire, we will ask participants to evaluate their own and the other player's performance during the learning task and state whether they complied with and benefited from the other player's choices. Further, we will ask participants how they felt when the other player received a good or a bad outcome. We will use this data for the descriptive part of the methods using non-parametric tests.

report: Reporting *p* values imprecisely (e.g., *p* < .05) reduces transparency, reproducibility, and re-use (e.g., in *p* value meta-analyses). Best practice is to report exact p-values with three decimal places (e.g., *p* = .032) unless *p* values are smaller than 0.001, in which case you can use *p* < .001.

The study conducted with adults was approved by the Ethics Committee of the Institute of Psychology at Humboldt-Universität zu Berlin (reference number 2022-65) and the study conducted with children by the Ethics Committee of the Institute of Psychology at the University of Greifswald (reference number BB 166/23).
live_data_statements: In the adult sample, seven participants were excluded (for details, see Woitow et al., 2026), resulting in a final sample of 79 adults (52 women; M = 23.80 years, SD = 4.12).
In the child sample, six participants were excluded due to an excessive number of missing responses in the learning and memory tasks (> 3 SDs above the group mean).
All participants had normal or corrected-to-normal vision, and children had no history of developmental disorders.
Written informed consent was obtained from adult participants and from children's parents, and children gave their assent before participation.

All participants completed the same experimental conditions in one session lasting approximately 70-80 minutes and were compensated with €10 per hour plus a bonus (€2 for adults, small gift for children).
Following the learning task, participants completed a surprise recognition memory test for images encountered during learning.
In both tasks, participants were instructed to collect as many points as possible and were told that the bonus depended on their performance.
To maximize points, participants had to learn the changing reward probabilities and adjust their choices accordingly.
To ensure attention, participants had to press the spacebar in OL trials to see the other player's choice.
Participants were introduced to the two image categories and shown example images for each.
Additionally, participants were advised to attend to trial values and images throughout the task.
At the end of the experiment, participants completed a questionnaire (Supporting Information: Debriefing questionnaire).
In the pilot, participants completed a learning task containing only 80 experiential learning trials.

text.text: Children's ability to learn and form memories through direct experience and observation increases with age.
However, the development of the underlying mechanisms, particularly prediction errors (PEs), through which both learning modes influence memory, remains unclear.

Using an incidental memory paradigm, we compared children (8-10 years) and adults (18-30 years) in how reward PEs (RPEs) during experiential and observational reinforcement learning affect episodic memory.
Although children showed weaker learning performance, both age groups remembered images better after experiential than after observational learning, and they did not differ in recognition accuracy.
However, adults showed greater memory strength and remembered images better when they or another player gambled for rewards, especially when associated with positive RPEs.
In contrast, children recognized images better when they rejected gambles, and exploratory analyses linked better memory to larger unsigned RPEs when they accepted gambles.
These findings suggest age differences in how one's own and observed decisions, and potentially associated reward predictions, shape episodic memory.

Observational learning plays a crucial role in cognitive and socio-emotional development (Bandura, 1977; Ishikawa & Itakura, 2024; Meltzoff, 2013; Waismeyer & Meltzoff, 2017) and is central to educational practice (Groenendijk et al., 2013).

text.text: The ability to learn and form memories through direct experience and observation continues to improve during middle childhood and adolescence (Ghetti & Bunge, 2012; Ofen, 2012; Westhoff et al., 2021; Xia et al., 2021).

text.text: These improvements are associated with more efficient use of learning strategies, better monitoring and control of memory (Ghetti & Bunge, 2012), and with memories becoming richer in detail (Ofen, 2012).
text.formatted: These improvements are associated with more efficient use of learning strategies, better monitoring and control of memory <ref type="bibr" target="#b29">(Ghetti & Bunge, 2012)</ref>, and with memories becoming richer in detail <ref type="bibr" target="#b51">(Ofen, 2012)</ref>.

text.text: Compared with adults, older children still learn more slowly and less efficiently from both direct experience and observation (Hämmerer et al., 2011; Rodriguez Buritica et al., 2018 , 2024) and show lower memory performance across learning contexts (Cycowicz et al., 2001; DeMaster et al., 2014; Ghetti & Bunge, 2012; Mecklinger et al., 2011).
text.formatted: Compared with adults, older children still learn more slowly and less efficiently from both direct experience and observation <ref type="bibr" target="#b37">(Hämmerer et al., 2011;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b60">Rodriguez Buritica et al., 2018</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b68">, 2024)</ref> and show lower memory performance across learning contexts <ref type="bibr" target="#b16">(Cycowicz et al., 2001;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b21">DeMaster et al., 2014;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b29">Ghetti & Bunge, 2012;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b45">Mecklinger et al., 2011)</ref>.

text.text: Moreover, although children are more sensitive to external feedback than adults, they struggle to extract task-relevant information from it (Eppinger et al., 2009; Hämmerer et al., 2011; Hämmerer & Eppinger, 2012; van den Bos et al., 2012).
text.formatted: Moreover, although children are more sensitive to external feedback than adults, they struggle to extract task-relevant information from it <ref type="bibr" target="#b24">(Eppinger et al., 2009;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b37">Hämmerer et al., 2011;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b36">Hämmerer & Eppinger, 2012;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b78">van den Bos et al., 2012)</ref>.

text.text: Learning from feedback requires individuals to evaluate outcomes and to update behavior accordingly.
This process is realized by prediction errors (PEs), defined as the difference between expected and received outcomes (Rescorla & Wagner, 1972; Sutton & Barto, 1998).
text.formatted: This process is realized by prediction errors (PEs), defined as the difference between expected and received outcomes <ref type="bibr" target="#b58">(Rescorla & Wagner, 1972;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b75">Sutton & Barto, 1998)</ref>.

text.text: PEs signal whether outcomes are better or worse than expected and are thought to be coded by midbrain dopamine neurons (Schultz, 2024; Schultz et al., 1997), which interact with a distributed network throughout the brain, including the striatum, anterior cingulate cortex, dorsolateral prefrontal cortex, and orbitofrontal cortex (Balleine et al., 2007; Behrens et al., 2007; Joiner et al., 2017; Schultz & Dickinson, 2000).
text.formatted: PEs signal whether outcomes are better or worse than expected and are thought to be coded by midbrain dopamine neurons <ref type="bibr" target="#b68">(Schultz, 2024;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b69">Schultz et al., 1997)</ref>, which interact with a distributed network throughout the brain, including the striatum, anterior cingulate cortex, dorsolateral prefrontal cortex, and orbitofrontal cortex <ref type="bibr" target="#b0">(Balleine et al., 2007;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">Behrens et al., 2007;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b41">Joiner et al., 2017;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b70">Schultz & Dickinson, 2000)</ref>.

text.text: As these regions undergo maturational changes during childhood and adolescence (Christakou et al., 2011; Crone et al., 2008), age differences in PE signaling are expected.
text.formatted: As these regions undergo maturational changes during childhood and adolescence <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">(Christakou et al., 2011;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b15">Crone et al., 2008)</ref>, age differences in PE signaling are expected.

text.text: However, empirical findings on PE signaling across development are mixed.

While some studies reported heightened neural PE signals in adolescents (Cohen et al., 2010; Davidow et al., 2016; Galvan et al., 2006), others found comparable PE-related neural activity across age groups (Rodriguez Buritica et al., 2024; van den Bos et al., 2012).
text.formatted: While some studies reported heightened neural PE signals in adolescents <ref type="bibr" target="#b14">(Cohen et al., 2010;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b18">Davidow et al., 2016;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b27">Galvan et al., 2006)</ref>, others found comparable PE-related neural activity across age groups <ref type="bibr" target="#b59">(Rodriguez Buritica et al., 2024;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b78">van den Bos et al., 2012)</ref>.

text.text: Nonetheless, computational research suggests that PEs drive both experiential and observational learning in adults and children (Burke et al., 2010; Joiner et al., 2017; Olsson et al., 2020; Rodriguez Buritica et al., 2024).
text.formatted: Nonetheless, computational research suggests that PEs drive both experiential and observational learning in adults and children <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">(Burke et al., 2010;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b41">Joiner et al., 2017;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b53">Olsson et al., 2020;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b59">Rodriguez Buritica et al., 2024)</ref>.

text.text: In adults, PEs during experiential learning have been shown to affect memory formation (Ergo et al., 2020; Pupillo & Bruckner, 2023), with most studies reporting encoding benefits of positive PEs (Calderon et al., 2021; De Loof et al., 2018; Jang et al., 2019; Rouhani et al., 2018; Rouhani & Niv, 2021).
text.formatted: In adults, PEs during experiential learning have been shown to affect memory formation <ref type="bibr" target="#b25">(Ergo et al., 2020;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b57">Pupillo & Bruckner, 2023)</ref>, with most studies reporting encoding benefits of positive PEs <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">(Calderon et al., 2021;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b19">De Loof et al., 2018;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b40">Jang et al., 2019;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b65">Rouhani et al., 2018;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b64">Rouhani & Niv, 2021)</ref>.

text.text: Our previous work further suggests that both experienced and vicarious positive PEs enhance memory strength (Woitow et al., 2026).
text.formatted: Our previous work further suggests that both experienced and vicarious positive PEs enhance memory strength <ref type="bibr">(Woitow et al., 2026)</ref>.

text.text: In contrast, few studies have investigated mnemonic effects of PEs across development, and findings are mixed, including positive effects of PEs (Breitwieser & Brod, 2021; Davidow et al., 2016), a Ushaped relation (Brod et al., 2022; Ortiz-Tudela et al., 2024), and no effects of PEs (Nolden et al., 2025).
text.formatted: In contrast, few studies have investigated mnemonic effects of PEs across development, and findings are mixed, including positive effects of PEs <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">(Breitwieser & Brod, 2021;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b18">Davidow et al., 2016)</ref>, a Ushaped relation <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">(Brod et al., 2022;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b54">Ortiz-Tudela et al., 2024)</ref>, and no effects of PEs <ref type="bibr" target="#b50">(Nolden et al., 2025)</ref>.

text.text: Although PEs often appear to enhance memory from late childhood onward, it remains unclear whether this benefit is comparable to that observed in adults (for a review, see Shing et al., 2023), and whether it generalizes to observational learning.
text.formatted: Although PEs often appear to enhance memory from late childhood onward, it remains unclear whether this benefit is comparable to that observed in adults (for a review, see <ref type="bibr" target="#b71">Shing et al., 2023)</ref>, and whether it generalizes to observational learning.

text.text: Moreover, recent computational research in adults showed that positive experienced and vicarious PEs elicited at the reward-predictive cue enhanced encoding, whereas outcome-related PEs did not (Jang et al., 2019; Woitow et al., 2026).
text.formatted: Moreover, recent computational research in adults showed that positive experienced and vicarious PEs elicited at the reward-predictive cue enhanced encoding, whereas outcome-related PEs did not <ref type="bibr" target="#b40">(Jang et al., 2019;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Woitow et al., 2026)</ref>.

text.text: As prior developmental work has focused on outcome-related PEs, it is unknown whether PEs at the reward-predictive cue play a comparable role in memory formation in children.
Taken together, the processes underlying the integration of information learned through experience and observation into episodic memories in middle childhood remain unclear.

To address this gap, the present study investigated how experiential and observational learning shape recognition memory in children aged 8-10 years compared with adults, focusing on the role of experienced and vicarious PEs.

We employed an incidental memory paradigm (Woitow et al., 2026) consisting of a learning task with interleaved experiential and observational trials, followed by an unexpected memory test for images shown in each learning condition (Figure 1a-b).
text.formatted: We employed an incidental memory paradigm <ref type="bibr">(Woitow et al., 2026)</ref> consisting of a learning task with interleaved experiential and observational trials, followed by an unexpected memory test for images shown in each learning condition (Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_1">1a-b</ref>).

text.text: In the learning task, participants learned reward probabilities for two image categories from trial-to-trial feedback.
On each trial, they either accepted or rejected the opportunity to gamble (experiential learning) or observed such a choice made by another player (observational learning).
To capture developmental differences, we compared data from the present study with those of our previous study, which used the same paradigm in young adults (18-30 years; Woitow et al., 2026).

text.text: We expected higher recognition accuracy following experiential learning (Ruggeri et al., 2019) and overall lower accuracy in children than in adults.

text.text: We further predicted age differences in choice behavior during learning, with better performance in adults (Rodriguez Buritica et al., 2018 , 2024; Topel et al., 2023).

text.text: Finally, to link learning and memory, we computed reward PEs (RPEs) during image and feedback presentation and analyzed their effects on memory.
In line with prior research, we expected children to learn from experienced and vicarious RPEs (Rodriguez Buritica et al., 2024).

text.text: Because brain regions involved in RPE coding and memory formation are still maturing (e.g., Crone et al., 2008; Ghetti & Bunge, 2012), we expected age differences in the effects of experienced and vicarious RPEs on memory formation.

text.text: However, given the mixed findings on the mnemonic effects of PEs in childhood (e.g., Nolden et al., 2025; Shing et al., 2023) and the lack of research on vicarious RPEs, we made no specific predictions regarding these differences.

text.text: We collected data from 86 children (46 girls) aged 8-10 years.

Children of this age still differ considerably from adults in how they use RPE signals during learning (e.g., van den Bos et al., 2012; van Duijvenvoorde et al., 2008), likely reflecting ongoing maturation of cortical and subcortical brain regions involved in RPE signaling and learning (Casey et al., 2005; Crone et al., 2008; Gogtay et al., 2004).

text.text: Following our adult study, we further assessed whether each participant's learning task performance exceeded chance level by simulating random choices using the same learning task structure and calculating the total score achieved.
This procedure was repeated 5,000 times.
All participants' scores were greater than 5% of the simulated score distribution.

Thus, the final sample consisted of 80 children (43 girls; M = 9.14 years, SD = 0.67), who were native German speakers recruited from urban and suburban populations in Greifswald, Germany, via the local population register (Melderegister MV) and local schools.

The adult study was approved by the Ethics Committee of the Institute of Psychology at Humboldt-Universität zu Berlin (2022-65) and the child study by the Ethics Committee of the Institute of Psychology at the University of Greifswald (BB 166/23).
All participants had normal or corrected-to-normal vision, and children had no history of developmental disorders.
Written informed consent was obtained from adult participants and from children's parents, and children gave their assent before participation.

All participants completed the same experimental conditions in one session lasting approximately 70-80 minutes and were compensated with €10 per hour plus a bonus (€2 for adults, small gift for children).
The study design, hypotheses, and planned analyses were preregistered (AsPredicted; #178674, https://aspredicted.org/qhs5-84qp.pdf).

RPE calculation.
The image RPE is the difference between the reward prediction after image presentation (e.g., 78) and before it (average across categories, e.g., 45).
The predicted reward per image category was computed for each trial from the values and probabilities of reward and punishment.
The feedback RPE is the difference between the received and the expected outcome.
The learning task comprised 160 interleaved experiential (EL) and observational (OL) learning trials (80 trials per condition, with no more than two consecutive trials of the same condition).
On each trial, participants accepted or rejected the opportunity to gamble for a probabilistic reward (EL) or observed such a choice made by another player (OL).
To maximize points, participants had to learn the changing reward probabilities and adjust their choices accordingly.
Each trial consisted of a player, value, image, and feedback phase, separated by 0.5-s blank screens (Figure 1a).
text.formatted: Each trial consisted of a player, value, image, and feedback phase, separated by 0.5-s blank screens (Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_1">1a</ref>).

text.text: First, the current player was cued ("You" for EL, "Other" for OL), followed by the trial value (i.e., reward magnitude; sampled equally from 1, 5, 10, 20, and 100).
Then, a unique image belonging to one of two possible categories -animate (animals) or inanimate (objects) -was shown with the options "Play" and "Pass" for 3 s.
Trial values and images were presented in pseudorandomized order, with animate and inanimate images occurring equally often in each learning condition and with each trial value.
The two image categories were associated with oppositely linked reward probabilities (e.g., 80% vs.
To accept or reject the gamble, participants chose "Play" or "Pass" within the 3-s window by pressing the left or right arrow key (positions randomized across participants).
To ensure attention, participants had to press the spacebar in OL trials to see the other player's choice.
Selected options were highlighted in black.
If no response was given, "Too slow" appeared, and the next trial started.
After the image phase, the feedback was shown for 1.5 s.
The current player was rewarded according to the trial's assigned reward probability.
Reward probabilities could change throughout the task to a random value between 0 and 1 with a likelihood of 0.16, while always remaining oppositely linked.
To enable learning, no changes occurred during the first 20 trials of the task or within 15 trials following a change (across EL and OL trials).
If the current player chose "Play" and the trial was rewarding, they received the points shown in the value phase.
If the trial was not rewarding, they always lost 10 points.
After passing, no points were won or lost, but the hypothetical outcome (i.e., the outcome for a play choice) was shown in brackets.
Notably, choices and feedback in OL trials did not affect the participant's score.
Finally, the current player's cumulative score was shown for 1 s.
Task instructions were read aloud to children, with examples of each trial phase and possible outcome (for the original German instructions, see Supporting Information: Task instructions).
Participants were introduced to the two image categories and shown example images for each.
An example task structure illustrated how the reward probabilities of the two image categories were related and how they changed across the task.
Additionally, participants were advised to attend to trial values and images throughout the task.
After the practice round, the rules of the learning task were summarized again.
In the memory task (Figure 1b), participants viewed all 160 images from the learning task intermixed with 160 matching new images (lures) in pseudorandomized order.
text.formatted: In the memory task (Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_1">1b</ref>), participants viewed all 160 images from the learning task intermixed with 160 matching new images (lures) in pseudorandomized order.

text.text: New images were different exemplars of the same animals or objects presented during learning.
On each trial, one image was shown, and participants indicated whether it was old or new by pressing the left or right arrow key (positions randomized across participants).
Participants received no feedback on response accuracy but were informed that 5 points would be added to their score for each correct response and 5 points subtracted for each incorrect response.
Following the old/new choice, participants rated their choice confidence on a scale from 1 (guess) to 4 (completely certain) by pressing the corresponding number key.
They had 5 s for each response type.
If no response was given, a prompt indicating that they were too slow was shown, and the next trial started immediately.
At the end of the experiment, participants completed a questionnaire (Supporting Information: Debriefing questionnaire).
Questionnaire items were read aloud to children.

On 5-point Likert scales, participants rated their understanding of the learning task rules, their own and the other player's learning performance, the extent to which they followed the observed choices and benefited from them, and how they felt when the other player received rewards or punishments.

Reward probabilities in all analyses refer to the expected reward probabilities estimated by the Bayesian ideal observer model (for details, see Supporting Information: Bayesian ideal observer model).

For all mixed-effects models (lme4 package, R; Bates et al., 2015), fixed effects were hypothesis-driven, and the random-effects structure was determined by model comparison (lowest BIC; for details, see Supporting Information: Model selection).

text.text: The predictors age group (adults, children), learning condition (EL, OL), choice (play, pass), confidence bin (low, high), and learning stage were treated as factors, while all other predictors were z-scored.
Participants' choice behavior in EL trials was analyzed using a logistic mixed-effects model.

Using singletrial data, we predicted the decision to play from age group, trial value, reward probability (P(rew)), and their interactions: The following analyses of learning behavior were exploratory.
First, we calculated each participant's ratio of play to pass choices as a measure of their overall tendency to gamble.
Second, we examined correct choices in the first eight EL trials of each learning stage (i.e., after task onset and after four reward probability changes).
We chose eight trials because this was the minimum number of EL trials (not counting interleaved OL trials) before the next change in reward probabilities across all participants and change points.

Choices were considered correct when participants played for images from the more frequently rewarded category (P(rew) > 0.5) or passed for images from the less frequently rewarded category (P(rew) < 0.5).
text.formatted: Choices were considered correct when participants played for images from the more frequently rewarded category (P(rew) > 0.5) or passed for images from the less frequently rewarded category (P(rew) < 0.5).

text.text: Correct choices were then modeled using a logistic mixed-effects model with the predictors age group, trial number, learning stage, and their interactions: (2) 𝑐𝑜𝑟𝑟𝑒𝑐𝑡 𝑐ℎ𝑜𝑖𝑐𝑒 ~ 𝑎𝑔𝑒 𝑔𝑟𝑜𝑢𝑝 * 𝑡𝑟𝑖𝑎𝑙 𝑛𝑢𝑚𝑏𝑒𝑟 * 𝑙𝑒𝑎𝑟𝑛𝑖𝑛𝑔 𝑠𝑡𝑎𝑔𝑒 + (1 + 𝑙𝑒𝑎𝑟𝑛𝑖𝑛𝑔 𝑠𝑡𝑎𝑔𝑒 | 𝑠𝑢𝑏𝑗𝑒𝑐𝑡).
Finally, we assessed whether participants made more correct choices following observational trials.

For each participant, we calculated the proportion of correct choices in these trials and compared it against chance (0.5) in each age group using a one-tailed one-sample t-test, and between age groups using a twosample t-test.
Memory accuracy was defined as the ability to discriminate old from new images.
We computed the discrimination index d′ (z(hit rate)z(false-alarm rate)) for each participant and learning condition.
Because old and new images were matching pairs showing the same kind of animal or object, false alarms were assigned to the learning condition of the matching old image.
Some children had false-alarm rates of 0 in some conditions, which would result in infinite d′ values.
Thus, hit and false-alarm rates were adjusted for all participants using the log-linear correction (Hautus, 1995).
text.formatted: Thus, hit and false-alarm rates were adjusted for all participants using the log-linear correction <ref type="bibr" target="#b38">(Hautus, 1995)</ref>.

text.text: One-sample t-tests against 0 tested whether accuracy exceeded chance in each learning condition and age group.

We then calculated d′ separately for play and pass trials, assigning false alarms to the choice made for the matching old image, and tested the effects of age group, learning condition, choice, and their interactions on d′ with a linear mixed-effects model: (3) 𝑑 ′ ~ 𝑎𝑔𝑒 𝑔𝑟𝑜𝑢𝑝 * 𝑙𝑒𝑎𝑟𝑛𝑖𝑛𝑔 𝑐𝑜𝑛𝑑𝑖𝑡𝑖𝑜𝑛 * 𝑐ℎ𝑜𝑖𝑐𝑒 + (1 | 𝑠𝑢𝑏𝑗𝑒𝑐𝑡).

In an exploratory analysis, we tested whether memory accuracy in EL trials depended on age group, choice, and each participant's play/pass ratio, controlling for overall learning task performance (final score): Moreover, we tested whether memory accuracy was higher when participants reported higher confidence in old/new judgments (ratings of 3 or 4) than lower confidence (ratings of 1 or 2).

A linear mixed-effects model predicted d′ from age group, learning condition, confidence bin, and their interactions: (5) 𝑑 ′ ~ 𝑎𝑔𝑒 𝑔𝑟𝑜𝑢𝑝 * 𝑙𝑒𝑎𝑟𝑛𝑖𝑛𝑔 𝑐𝑜𝑛𝑑𝑖𝑡𝑖𝑜𝑛 * 𝑐𝑜𝑛𝑓𝑖𝑑𝑒𝑛𝑐𝑒 𝑏𝑖𝑛 + (1 + 𝑐𝑜𝑛𝑓𝑖𝑑𝑒𝑛𝑐𝑒 𝑏𝑖𝑛 | 𝑠𝑢𝑏𝑗𝑒𝑐𝑡).
Next, we combined the old/new judgment and the confidence rating (1-4) per trial into a memory score ranging from 1 ("new" with highest confidence) to 8 ("old" with highest confidence).
To evaluate whether this score reflects memory strength, we examined its relation to the true proportion of old images.

The memory score and the proportion of old images showed a positive, near-linear relationship in both age groups and learning conditions (Figure S1), supporting its suitability as a measure of memory strength.

text.text: To test whether this relation differed between age groups, we modeled the proportion of old images as a function of age group, memory score, and their interaction: All subsequent analyses of memory strength used memory scores for old images.

Differences in memory strength between age groups and experimental conditions were assessed with a linear mixed-effects model predicting memory scores from age group, learning condition, choice, and their interactions: Because both age groups played more often for animate images (Table S33), we included image category as an additional predictor in exploratory memory models (for details, see Supporting Information: Effects of image category).

text.text: Participants' responses in the debriefing questionnaire were analyzed using nonparametric tests.
Both age groups reported overall good to very good rule understanding, although ratings were higher in adults (Figure S2).

text.text: To assess the credibility of our social manipulation, we examined participants' perception of the other player.
Most adults (75%) reported having benefited from observing the other player (ratings of 4 or 5), compared with fewer than half of the children (38%).

Moreover, adults rated their own choice performance similarly to that of the other player (p = 0.21, paired Wilcoxon signed-rank test), whereas children rated the other player's performance higher than their own (p < 0.001).

text.text: We computed reward prediction errors (RPEs) at image and feedback presentation in EL and OL trials (Figure 1c-d).
text.formatted: We computed reward prediction errors (RPEs) at image and feedback presentation in EL and OL trials (Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_1">1c-d</ref>).

text.text: The image RPE depended on trial value and reward probability (Figure 1c) and was the difference between the predicted reward after and before image presentation (Figure 1d).
text.formatted: The image RPE depended on trial value and reward probability (Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_1">1c</ref>) and was the difference between the predicted reward after and before image presentation (Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_1">1d</ref>).

text.text: The predicted reward on a given trial was calculated for each image category (animate, inanimate): 𝑉 𝑝𝑟𝑒𝑑 = 𝑉 𝑟𝑒𝑤 𝑃 𝑟𝑒𝑤 + 𝑉 𝑝𝑢𝑛 𝑃 𝑝𝑢𝑛 , where the predicted reward (𝑉 𝑝𝑟𝑒𝑑 ) is derived from the probability (𝑃 𝑟𝑒𝑤 ) and value (𝑉 𝑟𝑒𝑤 ) of reward, and the probability (𝑃 𝑝𝑢𝑛 ) and value (𝑉 𝑝𝑢𝑛 ; always -10) of punishment (Figure 1d).
text.formatted: The predicted reward on a given trial was calculated for each image category (animate, inanimate): 𝑉 𝑝𝑟𝑒𝑑 = 𝑉 𝑟𝑒𝑤 𝑃 𝑟𝑒𝑤 + 𝑉 𝑝𝑢𝑛 𝑃 𝑝𝑢𝑛 , where the predicted reward (𝑉 𝑝𝑟𝑒𝑑 ) is derived from the probability (𝑃 𝑟𝑒𝑤 ) and value (𝑉 𝑟𝑒𝑤 ) of reward, and the probability (𝑃 𝑝𝑢𝑛 ) and value (𝑉 𝑝𝑢𝑛 ; always -10) of punishment (Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_1">1d</ref>).

text.text: We assumed that the predicted reward before image presentation was the average across image categories.

The image RPE was then calculated by subtracting the average predicted reward (𝜇𝑉 𝑝𝑟𝑒𝑑 ) from the predicted reward for the displayed image category (𝑉 𝑝𝑟𝑒𝑑_𝑡ℎ𝑖𝑠𝐶𝑎𝑡 ): The feedback RPE depended on the trial outcome (win or loss; Figure 1c) and was the difference between the received outcome (𝑅(𝑡)) and the predicted reward for the displayed image category (Figure 1d): (11) 𝑓𝑒𝑒𝑑𝑏𝑎𝑐𝑘 𝑅𝑃𝐸 = 𝑅(𝑡) -𝑉 𝑝𝑟𝑒𝑑_𝑡ℎ𝑖𝑠𝐶𝑎𝑡 (𝑡).
text.formatted: The image RPE was then calculated by subtracting the average predicted reward (𝜇𝑉 𝑝𝑟𝑒𝑑 ) from the predicted reward for the displayed image category (𝑉 𝑝𝑟𝑒𝑑_𝑡ℎ𝑖𝑠𝐶𝑎𝑡 ): The feedback RPE depended on the trial outcome (win or loss; Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_1">1c</ref>) and was the difference between the received outcome (𝑅(𝑡)) and the predicted reward for the displayed image category (Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_1">1d</ref>): (11) 𝑓𝑒𝑒𝑑𝑏𝑎𝑐𝑘 𝑅𝑃𝐸 = 𝑅(𝑡) -𝑉 𝑝𝑟𝑒𝑑_𝑡ℎ𝑖𝑠𝐶𝑎𝑡 (𝑡).

text.text: To examine the effects of image and feedback RPEs on memory strength, we fitted linear regressions to memory scores and RPEs for each participant and condition.
Consistent with our previous study (Woitow et al., 2026), analyses focused on RPE valence.
text.formatted: Consistent with our previous study <ref type="bibr">(Woitow et al., 2026)</ref>, analyses focused on RPE valence.

text.text: RPEs were thus split by sign (RPE < 0, RPE > 0) before regressing the mean-centered memory scores on the mean RPE of each bin.
text.formatted: RPEs were thus split by sign (RPE < 0, RPE > 0) before regressing the mean-centered memory scores on the mean RPE of each bin.

text.text: For feedback RPEs, we tested actual feedback RPEs in play trials and, in an exploratory analysis, fictive feedback RPEs in pass trials (i.e., the difference between the hypothetical outcome and the predicted reward).

Effects on memory were assessed by testing the resulting slopes against zero using one-sample t-tests for each age group per choice and learning condition, with the α level Bonferroni-corrected for multiple comparisons.

We then tested the effects of age group, learning condition, choice, and their interactions on these slopes using linear mixed-effects models: Moreover, we explored the effect of unsigned image RPEs on memory in children.

For consistency with the other RPE analyses, unsigned image RPEs were split into two equal-sized bins (median split separately for play and pass trials), and regressions were fitted to memory scores and analyzed as described above.

To test whether this relationship depended on learning performance, we fitted a logistic regression per participant predicting play choices from reward probabilities and trial values, and computed a Spearman correlation between reward probability slopes (controlling for trial value) and the unsigned image RPEmemory slopes.
Finally, we explored unsigned feedback RPEs in play and pass trials in both age groups, using the same median split and slope analyses.
We assessed participants' learning performance by analyzing their play/pass choices.

Across age groups, the probability of accepting gambles (play choice) increased with trial value (Figure 2a; β = 0.79, z = 11.80, p < 0.001) and reward probability (P(rew); Figure 2b; β = 1.15, z = 19.51, p < 0.001; Table S1).
text.formatted: Across age groups, the probability of accepting gambles (play choice) increased with trial value (Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_7">2a</ref>; β = 0.79, z = 11.80, p < 0.001) and reward probability (P(rew); Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_7">2b</ref>; β = 1.15, z = 19.51, p < 0.001; Table <ref type="table">S1</ref>).

text.text: Both effects were stronger in adults than in children (age group × trial value: β = 0.38, z = 5.81, p < 0.001; age group × P(rew): β = 0.38, z = 6.47, p < 0.001), driven by group differences at lower reward probabilities (P(rew) ≤ 0.5; ps < 0.001) and smaller trial values (trial value ≤ 10; ps ≤ 0.004; Table S2).
text.formatted: Both effects were stronger in adults than in children (age group × trial value: β = 0.38, z = 5.81, p < 0.001; age group × P(rew): β = 0.38, z = 6.47, p < 0.001), driven by group differences at lower reward probabilities (P(rew) ≤ 0.5; ps < 0.001) and smaller trial values (trial value ≤ 10; ps ≤ 0.004; Table <ref type="table">S2</ref>).

text.text: Additionally, we found an age group × trial value × reward probability interaction (β = 0.08, z = 2.54, p = 0.011).

Follow-up analyses showed that the effect of trial value increased with reward probability in adults (β = 0.23, z = 4.17, p < 0.001; Table S3) but not in children (p = 0.83; Table S4), suggesting that adults integrated value and probability information more strongly.
text.formatted: Follow-up analyses showed that the effect of trial value increased with reward probability in adults (β = 0.23, z = 4.17, p < 0.001; Table <ref type="table">S3</ref>) but not in children (p = 0.83; Table <ref type="table">S4</ref>), suggesting that adults integrated value and probability information more strongly.

text.text: Finally, adults played less often than children (β = -0.13, z = -2.98, p = 0.003).
That is, they played in about 50% of the trials (mean play/pass ratio = 1.08) compared with 60% in children (mean ratio = 1.58).

These results suggest that both age groups used reward information to guide their play/pass choices, but children did so to a lesser extent, as their choices depended less on this information when reward values and probabilities were low.
Consistent with this, children achieved lower learning task scores (M = 575, SD = 212) than adults (M = 704, SD = 223; M diff = 129, 95% CI [61, 197], 𝑡157 = 3.73, p < 0.001, d = 0.59).

text.text: Moreover, we assessed reward probability learning by examining correct choices (i.e., playing for the more frequently rewarded and passing for the less frequently rewarded image category) in the first eight EL trials of each learning stage.

The probability of a correct choice increased across trials (β = 0.22, z = 7.85, p < 0.001), was higher in adults than in children (β = 0.17, z = 4.18, p < 0.001), and increased more steeply in adults (age group × trial: β = 0.12, z = 4.40, p < 0.001; Figure 2c).

text.text: This age difference varied with learning stage (age group × trial × learning stage: β = -0.07, z = -2.54, p = 0.011; Table S5), due to a flattening of the increase in correct choices in later learning stages in adults but not in children (trial × learning stage: adults: β = -0.10, z = -2.54, p = 0.011; children: p = 0.32; Tables S6-S7).

text.text: In sum, these findings indicate poorer reward probability learning and less optimal choice behavior in 8-to 10-year-olds than in young adults.
Next, we explored the influence of the other player's choices on participants' decisions.

We found that both age groups more often made correct choices after an OL trial (adults: M = 0.68, SD = 0.09, 95% CI [0.66, ∞], 𝑡78 = 17.56, p < 0.001, d = 1.98; children: M = 0.61, SD = 0.12, 95% CI [0.59, ∞], 𝑡79 = 8.72, p < 0.001, d = 0.98).

text.text: Nonetheless, the proportion of correct choices was higher in adults (M diff = 0.07, 95% CI [0.04, 0.10], 𝑡157 = 4.17, p < 0.001, d = 0.66), suggesting that adults integrated vicarious feedback more effectively than children.

text.text: Memory performance was first assessed by analyzing participants' accuracy in discriminating old from new images (d′).

Because lures were different exemplars of the same animals or objects as the old images, and false alarms were assigned to the condition and choice of the matching old image, d′ reflects how well participants distinguished studied images in each condition from their similar lures.
Memory accuracy was above chance in each learning condition and age group (adults: ts ≥ 23.55, ps < 0.001; children: ts ≥ 16.86, ps < 0.001; Figure S3).

text.text: Interestingly, children and adults did not differ in accuracy (β = -0.01, 𝑡157 = -0.39, p = 0.70; Figure 3a-b; Table S8), which was moderately supported by a Bayesian analysis (B01 = 3.36) and reflected in comparable final memory test scores (adults: M = 588, SD = 181; children: M = 538, SD = 279; M diff = 50, 95% CI [-24, 124], 𝑡157 = 1.34, p = 0.18, d = 0.21).

text.text: Age invariance in accuracy resulted from higher hit and false-alarm rates in adults (hits: β = 0.03, 𝑡157 = 3.30, p = 0.001; false alarms: β = 0.02, 𝑡157 = 2.20, p = 0.03), consistent with a more conservative response bias in children (Figure S4; Tables S9-S10).

text.text: Memory accuracy was higher in EL than in OL trials (β = 0.03, 𝑡471 = 2.18, p = 0.03), with no evidence for an age difference (age group × learning condition: β = -0.002, 𝑡471 = -0.17, p = 0.87), suggesting a comparable benefit of experiential learning in adults and children.

The effect of play/pass choice differed between age groups (β = 0.03, 𝑡471 = 2.49, p = 0.013), depending on the learning condition (age group × learning condition × choice: β = 0.03, 𝑡471 = 2.07, p = 0.04).
Follow-up analyses revealed overall greater accuracy in play than in pass trials in adults (choice: β = 0.04, 𝑡234 = 2.28, p = 0.024; Figure 3a; Table S11).

text.text: In contrast, children showed a learning condition × choice interaction (β = -0.05, 𝑡237 = -2.41, p = 0.017; Figure 3b; Table S12), due to higher accuracy for pass than for play trials in the EL condition (estimate = 0.15, 𝑡237 = 2.61, p = 0.01) but not in the OL condition (estimate = -0.04, 𝑡237 = -0.79, p = 0.43).

text.text: In addition, we explored whether the play/pass pattern in EL trials in adults and children was related to differences in play/pass ratios.
However, we found no evidence that memory accuracy for play and pass trials depended on the frequency of play and pass choices (p = 0.61; Table S14).

text.text: In the next step, we tested whether participants' confidence ratings reflected memory accuracy.

We found higher accuracy for high-than for low-confidence judgments (β = 0.37, 𝑡146 = 17.08, p < 0.001), which did not differ between age groups (confidence bin × age group: p = 0.57; Table S15), indicating that subjective confidence ratings reflected memory accuracy in adults and children.

Memory scores predicted the proportion of old images in both age groups (Figure 3c; β = 0.20, 𝑡157 = 35.11, p < 0.001), supporting their validity as a measure of memory strength.

text.text: Next, we examined whether a key reinforcement learning signal, the reward prediction error (RPE), influenced episodic memory, and whether this relationship differed between learning conditions and age groups.
Image RPE
The image RPE reflects the difference between the reward prediction after and before image presentation.
Slopes relating image RPE valence to memory strength did not differ from zero in any condition or age group (adults: ps ≥ 0.19; children: ps ≥ 0.58; Figure 4a-d; Table S18).

text.text: There was no effect of age group on these slopes (p = 0.99), and age group did not interact with learning condition or choice (ps ≥ 0.28; Table S19).
