text.text: Thus, signed experienced and vicarious image RPEs were not related to memory strength in either adults or children.
Following the exploratory analysis in our previous study (Woitow et al., 2026), we then examined memory strength separately for trials with positive and negative image RPEs.
text.formatted: Following the exploratory analysis in our previous study <ref type="bibr">(Woitow et al., 2026)</ref>, we then examined memory strength separately for trials with positive and negative image RPEs.

text.text: In adults, memory for play trials with positive image RPEs was above participants' average in both learning conditions (EL: M = 0.11, SD = 0.36, 95% CI [0.03, 0.19], 𝑡78 = 2.66, p = 0.009, d = 0.30; OL: M = 0.09, SD = 0.33, 95% CI [0.01, 0.16], 𝑡78 = 2.37, p = 0.02, d = 0.27; α corrected = 0.025), whereas children showed no such effect (ps ≥ 0.52; Table S20).
text.formatted: In adults, memory for play trials with positive image RPEs was above participants' average in both learning conditions (EL: M = 0.11, SD = 0.36, 95% CI [0.03, 0.19], 𝑡78 = 2.66, p = 0.009, d = 0.30; OL: M = 0.09, SD = 0.33, 95% CI [0.01, 0.16], 𝑡78 = 2.37, p = 0.02, d = 0.27; α corrected = 0.025), whereas children showed no such effect (ps ≥ 0.52; Table <ref type="table">S20</ref>).

text.text: Thus, positive image RPEs in play trials were associated with better memory in adults but not in children, although the effect did not differ significantly between age groups.
Building on prior work linking larger unsigned PEs to better memory in children (Breitwieser & Brod, 2021; Brod et al., 2022), we explored unsigned image RPEs in children.
text.formatted: Building on prior work linking larger unsigned PEs to better memory in children <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">(Breitwieser & Brod, 2021;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">Brod et al., 2022)</ref>, we explored unsigned image RPEs in children.

text.text: We found greater memory strength in EL play trials with larger than with smaller unsigned image RPEs (M = 0.02, SD = 0.07, 95% CI [0.005, 0.04], 𝑡79 = 2.58, p = 0.012, d = 0.29; α corrected = 0.0125), but not in OL or pass trials (ps ≥ 0.08; Table S21), suggesting that, when children gambled, more surprising reward cues may have benefited encoding more than less surprising ones.
text.formatted: We found greater memory strength in EL play trials with larger than with smaller unsigned image RPEs (M = 0.02, SD = 0.07, 95% CI [0.005, 0.04], 𝑡79 = 2.58, p = 0.012, d = 0.29; α corrected = 0.0125), but not in OL or pass trials (ps ≥ 0.08; Table <ref type="table">S21</ref>), suggesting that, when children gambled, more surprising reward cues may have benefited encoding more than less surprising ones.

text.text: This association was stronger in children whose choices were more sensitive to reward probabilities (Spearman's ρ = 0.24, p = 0.03).
Moreover, mnemonic effects of signed RPEs elicited by the reward outcome were assessed.

Neither actual feedback RPEs in play trials nor, in exploratory analyses, fictive feedback RPEs in pass trials were related to memory strength in either age group or learning condition (play: ps ≥ 0.054; pass: ps ≥ 0.20; α corrected = 0.0125; Figure S6; Table S22).
text.formatted: Neither actual feedback RPEs in play trials nor, in exploratory analyses, fictive feedback RPEs in pass trials were related to memory strength in either age group or learning condition (play: ps ≥ 0.054; pass: ps ≥ 0.20; α corrected = 0.0125; Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_18">S6</ref>; Table <ref type="table">S22</ref>).

text.text: These slopes did not differ between age groups or learning conditions (ps ≥ 0.44), but they were more positive for actual than fictive feedback RPEs (β = 0.004, 𝑡471 = 3.09, p = 0.002), driven by a negative slope for fictive feedback RPEs across age groups and learning conditions (𝑡423 = -2.60, p = 0.01, d = -0.15; α corrected = 0.025), whereas actual feedback RPEs were unrelated to memory (p = 0.13; Table S23).
text.formatted: These slopes did not differ between age groups or learning conditions (ps ≥ 0.44), but they were more positive for actual than fictive feedback RPEs (β = 0.004, 𝑡471 = 3.09, p = 0.002), driven by a negative slope for fictive feedback RPEs across age groups and learning conditions (𝑡423 = -2.60, p = 0.01, d = -0.15; α corrected = 0.025), whereas actual feedback RPEs were unrelated to memory (p = 0.13; Table <ref type="table">S23</ref>).

text.text: Thus, signed feedback RPEs in play trials did not affect memory, whereas positive fictive feedback RPEs (i.e., missed wins) might have reduced memory strength.

Finally, exploratory analyses of unsigned feedback RPEs showed no reliable effects (play: ps ≥ 0.02; pass: ps ≥ 0.25; α corrected = 0.0125; Table S24), and no differences between age groups, learning conditions, or choices (ps ≥ 0.11; Table S25), suggesting that the magnitude of actual and fictive feedback RPEs did not affect memory.
text.formatted: Finally, exploratory analyses of unsigned feedback RPEs showed no reliable effects (play: ps ≥ 0.02; pass: ps ≥ 0.25; α corrected = 0.0125; Table <ref type="table">S24</ref>), and no differences between age groups, learning conditions, or choices (ps ≥ 0.11; Table <ref type="table">S25</ref>), suggesting that the magnitude of actual and fictive feedback RPEs did not affect memory.

text.text: The present study used an incidental memory paradigm to examine developmental differences between 8-to 10-year-old children and young adults in how reward prediction errors (RPEs) during experiential and observational reinforcement learning affect episodic memory.
Although children's choices were less optimal than adults', both age groups used reward information to guide their choices and benefited from observing another player.
Across age groups, memory accuracy and strength were higher after experiential than after observational learning.
Memory accuracy was comparable between age groups, whereas adults showed greater memory strength.
Additionally, choice effects on memory differed between age groups.
Finally, in adults, positive image RPEs in experienced and observed play trials were associated with enhanced memory strength.
In children, larger unsigned image RPEs in experienced play trials were linked to better memory.
Adults' and children's play/pass choices indicated that they attended to reward information and used it to guide gambling behavior.
However, children played more often than adults on trials with low reward values and probabilities, resulting in lower learning task scores.

This suggests that children had difficulties forming accurate representations of task-appropriate behavior (Eppinger et al., 2009) and supports prior research showing that primary school children partially neglect reward probabilities when making decisions (Lang & Betsch, 2018).
text.formatted: This suggests that children had difficulties forming accurate representations of task-appropriate behavior <ref type="bibr" target="#b24">(Eppinger et al., 2009)</ref> and supports prior research showing that primary school children partially neglect reward probabilities when making decisions <ref type="bibr" target="#b42">(Lang & Betsch, 2018)</ref>.

text.text: Accordingly, children's proportion of correct choices increased less over the course of learning, consistent with evidence for less efficient probabilistic reinforcement learning in children (Topel et al., 2023; Westhoff et al., 2021; Xia et al., 2021).
text.formatted: Accordingly, children's proportion of correct choices increased less over the course of learning, consistent with evidence for less efficient probabilistic reinforcement learning in children <ref type="bibr" target="#b77">(Topel et al., 2023;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b81">Westhoff et al., 2021;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b83">Xia et al., 2021)</ref>.

text.text: Notably, reward probabilities in our study changed repeatedly.
Although exploratory analyses indicated that children, like adults, detected these changes and adjusted their choices accordingly (Table S26), they made fewer correct choices overall.
text.formatted: Although exploratory analyses indicated that children, like adults, detected these changes and adjusted their choices accordingly (Table <ref type="table">S26</ref>), they made fewer correct choices overall.

text.text: This aligns with studies showing lower choice accuracy in children than in adults when reward probabilities are non-stationary (for a review, see Topel et al., 2023).
text.formatted: This aligns with studies showing lower choice accuracy in children than in adults when reward probabilities are non-stationary (for a review, see <ref type="bibr" target="#b77">Topel et al., 2023)</ref>.

text.text: Both age groups also adjusted their choices to recent outcomes, but children did so less (Table S27), mainly because they used hypothetical losses less (Figure S7; Table S28), consistent with evidence that counterfactual outcome integration continues to develop into adolescence (Palminteri et al., 2016).
text.formatted: Both age groups also adjusted their choices to recent outcomes, but children did so less (Table <ref type="table">S27</ref>), mainly because they used hypothetical losses less (Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_19">S7</ref>; Table <ref type="table">S28</ref>), consistent with evidence that counterfactual outcome integration continues to develop into adolescence <ref type="bibr" target="#b55">(Palminteri et al., 2016)</ref>.

text.text: Children's weaker use of hypothetical losses may have contributed to their more frequent play choices and lower learning task scores.

Moreover, although both age groups benefited from observing the other player's feedback, adults made more correct choices after observational trials, consistent with evidence for developmental differences in using vicarious information for learning (Rodriguez Buritica et al., 2018 , 2024).
text.formatted: Moreover, although both age groups benefited from observing the other player's feedback, adults made more correct choices after observational trials, consistent with evidence for developmental differences in using vicarious information for learning <ref type="bibr" target="#b60">(Rodriguez Buritica et al., 2018</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b68">, 2024)</ref>.

text.text: Despite these age differences in learning performance, recognition accuracy did not differ between age groups.
This contradicts our hypothesis and prior research showing better picture recognition in adults (Cycowicz et al., 2001; Czernochowski et al., 2005; Friedman et al., 2010; Sprondel et al., 2011).
text.formatted: This contradicts our hypothesis and prior research showing better picture recognition in adults <ref type="bibr" target="#b16">(Cycowicz et al., 2001;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b17">Czernochowski et al., 2005;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b26">Friedman et al., 2010;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b73">Sprondel et al., 2011)</ref>.

text.text: However, the findings match other studies reporting age-invariant recognition accuracy in young adults and children aged 8 and older (Billingsley et al., 2002; Brainerd et al., 2004; Ofen et al., 2007).
text.formatted: However, the findings match other studies reporting age-invariant recognition accuracy in young adults and children aged 8 and older <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">(Billingsley et al., 2002;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">Brainerd et al., 2004;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b52">Ofen et al., 2007)</ref>.

text.text: Notably, because these studies vary in experimental design (e.g., explicit instructions to memorize items or repeated memory item presentation), comparisons should be made with caution.

Overall, our findings provide evidence that young adults and 8-to 10-year-olds are similarly accurate in recognizing incidentally encoded images from experiential and observational learning and in discriminating them from similar lures.

Given that adults often show better recognition, this finding may reflect a tendency in adults to miss details (e.g., image features) due to greater selective attention to task-relevant information (e.g., image category) relative to children (Blanco et al., 2023; Tandoc et al., 2024).
text.formatted: Given that adults often show better recognition, this finding may reflect a tendency in adults to miss details (e.g., image features) due to greater selective attention to task-relevant information (e.g., image category) relative to children <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">(Blanco et al., 2023;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b76">Tandoc et al., 2024)</ref>.

text.text: Taking subjective confidence into account, however, revealed greater memory strength in adults than in children, consistent with prior work (Friedman et al., 2010; Ghetti & Angelini, 2008; Ghetti & Bunge, 2012).
text.formatted: Taking subjective confidence into account, however, revealed greater memory strength in adults than in children, consistent with prior work <ref type="bibr" target="#b26">(Friedman et al., 2010;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b28">Ghetti & Angelini, 2008;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b29">Ghetti & Bunge, 2012)</ref>.

text.text: That age differences emerged in memory strength but not in memory accuracy may reflect distinct developmental trajectories of the two processes of recognition memory: familiarity and recollection (for a review, see Ghetti & Angelini, 2008).
text.formatted: That age differences emerged in memory strength but not in memory accuracy may reflect distinct developmental trajectories of the two processes of recognition memory: familiarity and recollection (for a review, see <ref type="bibr" target="#b28">Ghetti & Angelini, 2008)</ref>.

text.text: Familiarity (recognizing an event without retrieving details) is thought to reach adult levels by about 8 years of age, whereas recollection (retrieving qualitative details of the study episode) continues to develop into young adulthood (Billingsley et al., 2002; Brainerd et al., 2004; Ghetti & Angelini, 2008).
text.formatted: Familiarity (recognizing an event without retrieving details) is thought to reach adult levels by about 8 years of age, whereas recollection (retrieving qualitative details of the study episode) continues to develop into young adulthood <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">(Billingsley et al., 2002;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">Brainerd et al., 2004;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b28">Ghetti & Angelini, 2008)</ref>.

text.text: Although d′ has been linked to familiarity (Yonelinas et al., 2024) and highconfidence recognition to recollection (Yonelinas & Parks, 2007), high confidence can also reflect strong familiarity (Migo et al., 2012).
text.formatted: Although d′ has been linked to familiarity <ref type="bibr" target="#b85">(Yonelinas et al., 2024)</ref> and highconfidence recognition to recollection <ref type="bibr" target="#b84">(Yonelinas & Parks, 2007)</ref>, high confidence can also reflect strong familiarity <ref type="bibr" target="#b47">(Migo et al., 2012)</ref>.

text.text: Hence, our paradigm cannot clearly dissociate recollection-and familiaritybased contributions to memory strength.

In middle childhood, the ability to monitor and control one's own memory, that is, metamemory (Dunlosky & Thiede, 2013; Nelson, 1990), is present but still developing (Ghetti et al., 2008 (Ghetti et al., , 2011)).
text.formatted: In middle childhood, the ability to monitor and control one's own memory, that is, metamemory <ref type="bibr" target="#b23">(Dunlosky & Thiede, 2013;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b49">Nelson, 1990)</ref>, is present but still developing <ref type="bibr">(Ghetti et al., 2008</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b32">(Ghetti et al., , 2011))</ref>.

text.text: Accordingly, children's confidence judgments reflect their memory accuracy more closely with increasing age (Ghetti et al., 2010 (Ghetti et al., , 2011;; Ghetti & Angelini, 2008; Roebers et al., 2009), which is associated with improvements in executive functions and metacognition (Roebers, 2017).
text.formatted: Accordingly, children's confidence judgments reflect their memory accuracy more closely with increasing age <ref type="bibr" target="#b30">(Ghetti et al., 2010</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b32">(Ghetti et al., , 2011;;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b28">Ghetti & Angelini, 2008;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b62">Roebers et al., 2009)</ref>, which is associated with improvements in executive functions and metacognition <ref type="bibr" target="#b61">(Roebers, 2017)</ref>.

text.text: Consistent with this, higher confidence was associated with higher memory accuracy in both age groups, but memory scores tracked the true proportion of old images more closely in adults, suggesting more accurate metacognitive monitoring.
Taken together, our findings suggest that although 8-to 10-year-old children and young adults show comparable recognition accuracy, adults are better able to monitor their own memory.
As predicted, recognition memory was better after experiential than after observational learning in both age groups, as reflected in memory accuracy and in memory strength.

Given that confidence ratings in both age groups reflected recognition accuracy, these results suggest that one's own experiences facilitate encoding of image or context details, thereby enhancing memory accuracy and strength in children and adults.
This aligns with the assumption that active, self-directed learning leads to richer representations of study details than passive observation (Markant et al., 2016).
text.formatted: This aligns with the assumption that active, self-directed learning leads to richer representations of study details than passive observation <ref type="bibr" target="#b43">(Markant et al., 2016)</ref>.

text.text: Research in adults further showed that simply choosing between two options enhances memory (Ding et al., 2021; Murty et al., 2015).
text.formatted: Research in adults further showed that simply choosing between two options enhances memory <ref type="bibr" target="#b22">(Ding et al., 2021;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b48">Murty et al., 2015)</ref>.

text.text: Accordingly, making play/pass choices may have contributed to mnemonic benefits of experiential learning in both age groups.

Overall, these findings support evidence from adult and developmental studies reporting better memory following active, compared with observational, learning (Gureckis & Markant, 2012; Markant et al., 2016; Ruggeri et al., 2019 Ruggeri et al., , 2025)).
text.formatted: Overall, these findings support evidence from adult and developmental studies reporting better memory following active, compared with observational, learning <ref type="bibr" target="#b35">(Gureckis & Markant, 2012;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b43">Markant et al., 2016;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b67">Ruggeri et al., 2019</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b66">Ruggeri et al., , 2025))</ref>.

text.text: Interestingly, play/pass choices affected memory differently in adults and children.
In adults, both experienced and observed gambling enhanced memory accuracy and strength compared to passing.

Given that rewards were probabilistic, this suggests that risk and outcome uncertainty associated with gambling for rewards benefited encoding (Jang et al., 2019; Rouhani et al., 2018; Stanek et al., 2019).
text.formatted: Given that rewards were probabilistic, this suggests that risk and outcome uncertainty associated with gambling for rewards benefited encoding <ref type="bibr" target="#b40">(Jang et al., 2019;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b65">Rouhani et al., 2018;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b74">Stanek et al., 2019)</ref>.

text.text: The comparable effect across learning conditions indicates that adults encoded experienced and observed choices similarly (Woitow et al., 2026), in line with the assumption of similar neural activation during the generation, imagination, and observation of actions (Decety & Grèzes, 2006).
text.formatted: The comparable effect across learning conditions indicates that adults encoded experienced and observed choices similarly <ref type="bibr">(Woitow et al., 2026)</ref>, in line with the assumption of similar neural activation during the generation, imagination, and observation of actions <ref type="bibr" target="#b20">(Decety & Grèzes, 2006)</ref>.

text.text: In children, choice effects differed between learning conditions.

Observed choices did not affect memory accuracy, but in the experiential condition, accuracy was higher for pass than for play trials, suggesting that children encoded their own choices differently from adults.
One explanation could be that because children played more often than they passed, the fewer pass trials were more salient.
However, we found no evidence that the play/pass difference in accuracy depended on participants' play/pass ratios.
Alternatively, children might have deliberated longer when passing and thus attended to the image longer, as suggested by their slower responses in pass trials (Table S29).
text.formatted: Alternatively, children might have deliberated longer when passing and thus attended to the image longer, as suggested by their slower responses in pass trials (Table <ref type="table">S29</ref>).

text.text: However, within participants, slower responses were associated with fewer hits in both age groups (Table S30), arguing against this account.
text.formatted: However, within participants, slower responses were associated with fewer hits in both age groups (Table <ref type="table">S30</ref>), arguing against this account.

text.text: Another possibility is that, when children played, anticipating the upcoming outcome and reward uncertainty drew attention away from the image.
Future studies could disentangle these effects by using eye tracking and physiological measures to track attention and arousal during decision-making.

In sum, our results are consistent with evidence that different cognitive processes, such as decisionmaking, probabilistic reinforcement learning, and recognition memory, follow distinct developmental trajectories.

While familiarity-based recognition appears to be adult-like by the age of 8 (for a review, see Ghetti & Angelini, 2008), the ability to adjust decision-making based on reward cues and feedback in nonstationary, probabilistic environments improves into adolescence (Christakou et al., 2013; Topel et al., 2023; Xia et al., 2021).
text.formatted: While familiarity-based recognition appears to be adult-like by the age of 8 (for a review, see <ref type="bibr" target="#b28">Ghetti & Angelini, 2008)</ref>, the ability to adjust decision-making based on reward cues and feedback in nonstationary, probabilistic environments improves into adolescence <ref type="bibr" target="#b13">(Christakou et al., 2013;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b77">Topel et al., 2023;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b83">Xia et al., 2021)</ref>.

text.text: Future studies spanning a broader developmental range will be needed to delineate the timelines of these partially dissociable processes.

To further examine how experiential and observational learning shape episodic memory, we assessed the role of experienced and vicarious RPEs at the reward-predictive cue (image RPE) and the reward outcome (feedback RPE).

In adults, positive image RPEs in play trials were associated with enhanced memory strength in both learning conditions, suggesting a similar role of experienced and vicarious RPEs in memory encoding (Woitow et al., 2026).
text.formatted: In adults, positive image RPEs in play trials were associated with enhanced memory strength in both learning conditions, suggesting a similar role of experienced and vicarious RPEs in memory encoding <ref type="bibr">(Woitow et al., 2026)</ref>.

text.text: In children, we found no evidence for this effect in either learning condition.
Although this may suggest developmental differences in the role of signed RPEs, the effect did not differ significantly between age groups, so this conclusion remains tentative.
The absence of an effect in children may also reflect their still-developing ability to form accurate reward predictions.
In our task, predicting rewards required combining the probability and magnitude of potential rewards and losses.
Children's choices depended on both trial value and reward probability, but unlike adults, they showed no evidence of combining the two.
If children weighted these components differently than our model assumed, image RPEs may not fully capture RPE signaling in 8-to 10-year-olds.
However, exploratory analyses showed that children's play choices were sensitive to both the predicted reward value and the image RPE, although less strongly than adults' choices (Tables S31-S32).
text.formatted: However, exploratory analyses showed that children's play choices were sensitive to both the predicted reward value and the image RPE, although less strongly than adults' choices (Tables <ref type="table">S31-S32</ref>).

text.text: Thus, despite their difficulties in forming accurate reward predictions, children's choices tracked trial-by-trial changes in these predictions.

Exploratory analyses further showed that, in children, larger unsigned image RPEs were associated with greater memory strength in experienced play trials, particularly in children whose choices were more sensitive to reward probabilities.
Thus, when children gambled for rewards, larger deviations from their reward predictions may have benefited encoding more than smaller deviations.

Future research should replicate this finding and test, for example with pupillometry, whether responses to prediction violations scale with RPE magnitude and predict subsequent memory (Breitwieser & Brod, 2021; Brod et al., 2022).
text.formatted: Future research should replicate this finding and test, for example with pupillometry, whether responses to prediction violations scale with RPE magnitude and predict subsequent memory <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">(Breitwieser & Brod, 2021;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">Brod et al., 2022)</ref>.

text.text: Finally, we found no reliable evidence that signed or unsigned feedback RPEs in play or pass trials influenced memory in either age group or learning condition, although, across age groups and learning conditions, memory was worse for images followed by missed wins than by avoided losses.
This may reflect post-encoding interference due to attention to and processing of hypothetical wins and may further suggest similar processing of one's own and others' outcomes in both age groups.

Overall, these findings suggest that feedback RPEs may not enhance encoding when they do not coincide with the presentation of memory items (Jang et al., 2019; Rouhani & Niv, 2021; Woitow et al., 2026).
text.formatted: Overall, these findings suggest that feedback RPEs may not enhance encoding when they do not coincide with the presentation of memory items <ref type="bibr" target="#b40">(Jang et al., 2019;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b64">Rouhani & Niv, 2021;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Woitow et al., 2026)</ref>.

text.text: A limitation of the present study is the lack of behavioral measures in the observational learning condition to assess vicarious reward predictions.

Future studies could address this by including catch trials requiring participants to predict the other player's choices or outcomes, which would also verify attention to reward information during observational trials.
Notably, we used the same paradigm in adults and children to ensure comparability.

Considering that children made less accurate reward predictions, future studies could reduce the number of different reward values and use more distinct reward probabilities, which might facilitate the formation of accurate reward predictions and hence RPE effects.
In summary, the present study reveals developmental differences in how experiential and observational reinforcement learning shape episodic memory.
Adults chose more optimally during learning than children.
Moreover, adults' memory accuracy was higher for accepted gambles (own and observed), whereas children's was higher when they rejected them.
In adults, positive image RPEs during experienced and observed gambling were associated with better memory.
In children, exploratory analyses linked better memory to larger unsigned image RPEs during experienced gambling.
Given that feedback RPEs did not enhance memory in either age group, RPEs may enhance encoding only when temporally aligned with item presentation.

Together, our findings suggest that children can learn from their own and others' experiences in changing environments and adjust their behavior accordingly, although their less accurate reward predictions may affect how the resulting prediction errors shape their memory.

In this task, each trial consists of four phases: player, value, image, and feedback.
During the player phase, you will be informed on whose turn it is to gamble on the current trial, indicated by either YOU or OTHER (more on this later in the instructions).
Next, you will see a value (1, 5, 10, 20, or 100), followed by a unique image.
Whether the left option is PLAY or PASS will be randomly assigned at the beginning of the task and be the same afterward.
You will have 3 seconds to make your choice.
If you do not respond within the time limit you will see the message "Too slow!"
and the next trial will start immediately.
After choosing, you will receive feedback.
Here is an example of the trial structure:
Your goal is to maximize your points from playing the game.
Your points will be converted to BONUS PAYMENTS when you finish the entire experiment.
Your accumulated points will be shown at the end of every trial.
Here are the rules:
The value shown before the image tells you how much the current trial is worth.
Your choice made during the image presentation will be highlighted in black.
After choosing to play or to pass, each trial will give a reward at a certain probability.
This probability will change abruptly from time to time.
If you PLAY and the trial is REWARDING, you will be rewarded by the value presented at the beginning of the trial.
For example, if a trial is worth 20 pts and you choose to play, you would gain 20 pts.
However, if you PLAY but the trial is NOT REWARDING, you will always lose 10 pts.
Whether the left option is OLD or NEW will be randomly assigned at the beginning of the task and will be the same afterward.
For example, you've seen this whale before, so you should choose OLD:
However, you haven't seen THIS whale, so you should choose NEW:
You will have 5 seconds to decide.
If you do not respond within the time limit you will see the message "Too slow!"
and the next trial will start.
Once you have determined whether an image is old or new, you will be asked HOW CONFIDENT you are of that decision.
You will be given 4 choices for this rating (1 -guess, 2 -somewhat certain, 3 -quite certain, 4 -completely certain):
Press the CORRESPONDING NUMBER on your keyboard to choose your confidence.
You will have 5 seconds to give a response.
For example, if you chose OLD, but you guessed it, then press 1.
If you chose OLD and vividly remember seeing the image, then press 4.
Use 2 or 3 if your confidence is somewhere in between.
In this task, you will NOT receive FEEDBACK about your choice.
Nevertheless, every time you make a CORRECT choice, 5 points will be added to your score (+5).
For every INCORRECT choice, 5 points will be subtracted from your score (-5).
Your confidence rating will NOT affect your score, so please answer honestly.
Remember, your total score will be converted to BONUS PAYMENTS when you finish the entire experiment.
This part will take about 20 minutes.

text.text: To simulate realistic, human-like choice behavior for the observational learning (OL) condition, we fitted two RL models -our base model and an extended model -directly to the choice behavior from 30 young adults (18-30 years) who participated in the pilot phase of our adult study.
In the pilot, participants completed a learning task containing only 80 experiential learning trials.

The base model contained four free parameters: (1) a temperature parameter (inverse T) of the softmax function, (2) a value exponent term that scales the effect of trial value on choice behavior, (3) a play bias term reflecting the attribution of higher value to play decisions, and (4) an intercept term that scales the effect of learning rate on choice behavior.

The extended model contained the same free parameters as our base model and included two additional ones, surprise and uncertainty, which contributed to the trial-to-trial modulation of the learning rate.
Next, we assessed model fits by computing the Bayesian information criterion (BIC) for each model and then comparing them.
Since BIC values indicated that both models performed similarly well, we chose the simpler model (base model) to generate the choices for the OL condition.
For this, we used the model-derived expected trial value (𝑉 𝐵 (𝑡)) and the temperature parameter estimates as inputs to the softmax function to generate a choice for each trial.
We used the base RL model derived from the pilot sample for the adult study to simulate choice behavior for the OL condition in the child study.
This approach ensured that the observed choice behavior was comparable across participants and studies.

We used the same Bayesian ideal observer model as in the prior adult study (Woitow et al., 2026) to estimate the likelihood of a binary outcome (reward, no reward) on each trial while accounting for changes in the reward probabilities.
text.formatted: We used the same Bayesian ideal observer model as in the prior adult study <ref type="bibr">(Woitow et al., 2026)</ref> to estimate the likelihood of a binary outcome (reward, no reward) on each trial while accounting for changes in the reward probabilities.

text.text: Importantly, participants received information about trial outcomes regardless of the learning condition.
Therefore, we applied the ideal observer model in both learning conditions to compute the expected reward rate, surprise, uncertainty, and ideal learning rate.
As model input, we provided the binary outcome of each trial and the true probability of a reward probability change (change point, CP) occurring on any given trial (hazard rate, H).
The hazard rate was computed per participant by dividing the number of reward probability change points by the total number of trials.
The model assumes that a change point occurs on each trial with probability H. If no change point occurs, the reward rate (𝜇 𝑡 ) remains the same as on the previous trial (𝜇 𝑡-1 ).
If a change point occurs, a new reward rate is drawn from a uniform distribution between 0 and 1.
The current belief about the reward rate (𝑉(𝑡 + 1)) resulted from the previous reward rate belief (𝑉(𝑡)), the ideal learning rate 𝛼, and the prediction error (𝑃𝐸).
PE was computed as the difference between the obtained outcome (𝑅(𝑡)) and the predicted outcome (𝑉(𝑡)).

Task procedure and reward computations. a.
Learning task.

Each trial followed the same procedure: (1) the current player cue (You: experiential learning, EL; Other: observational learning, OL), (2) the trial value (e.g., 100), (3) a trial-unique image reflecting the reward probability, upon which the current player (EL: participant; OL: computer-generated other player) chose to play (accept the gamble) or to pass (reject the gamble), (4) the feedback showing the earnings after playing or the hypothetical outcome after passing, and (5) the current player's cumulative score. b.
Memory task.
Participants saw the images from the learning task intermixed with lures and judged whether each was old or new before rating their confidence. c.
Reward prediction errors (RPEs).
The trial value was sampled equally from[1, 5, 10, 20, 100].
The image RPE resulted from the reward probability (e.g., 0.8 and 0.2) and value (e.g., 100 and 20).
The feedback RPE depended on the outcome. d.
RPE calculation.
The image RPE is the difference between the reward prediction after image presentation (e.g., 78) and before it (average across categories, e.g., 45).
The predicted reward per image category was computed for each trial from the values and probabilities of reward and punishment.
The feedback RPE is the difference between the received and the expected outcome.

Oxford University Press. https://doi.org/10.1093/oxfordhb/9780190917982.013.32 Phasen: Spieler, Wert, Bild und Ergebnis. Zu Beginn eines Durchgangs erfährst du, wer an der Reihe ist. Wenn du das Wort "Du" siehst, bist du dran. Wenn du das Wort "Anderer" siehst, ist ein anderer Spieler dran und du schaust zu. Dann siehst du einen Wert (1, 5, 10, 20 oder 100) und danach ein Bild und die beiden Optionen "Spielen" und "Passen". Wenn du dran bist, musst du dich, wenn du das Bild siehst, zwischen "Spielen" und "Passen" entscheiden. Hierzu drückst du die rechte oder linke Pfeiltaste (auf entsprechende Tasten verweisen). Drück die linke Pfeiltaste für die linke Option und die rechte Pfeiltaste für die rechte Option. Schau bitte am Anfang der Aufgabe genau hin auf welcher Seite welche Option gezeigt wird. Was du auswählst, wird in schwarz hervorgehoben.

Das Bild wird immer für 3 Sekunden gezeigt. So lange hast du Zeit dich zwischen "Spielen" und "Passen" zu entscheiden. Spielen bedeutet, dass du um die Punkte, die du zuvor gesehen hast, spielen möchtest. Passen bedeutet, dass du nicht um die Punkte spielen möchtest. Wenn die Zeit vorbei ist und du nicht geantwortet hast, wird dir die Nachricht "Zu langsam!" angezeigt. Danach beginnt der nächste Durchgang. Es ist sehr wichtig, dass du versucht immer rechtzeitig zu antworten. Wenn du dich zwischen "Spielen" und "Passen" entschieden hast, wird dir das Ergebnis des Durchgangs angezeigt. Hier ist ein Beispiel für den Ablauf eines Durchgangs: (Nochmal auf einzelne Phasen verweisen)

Dein Ziel bei dieser Aufgabe ist es möglichst viele Punkte zu sammeln. Wenn du fleißig Punkte sammelst, erhältst du am Ende der Testung ein kleines Geschenk. Am Ende jedes Durchgangs werden dir deine bisher gesammelten Punkte angezeigt. Hier sind die Spielregeln: Die Zahl am Anfang gibt an wie viele Punkte du gewinnen kannst. Ob du die Punkte bekommst, erfährst du, nachdem du "Spielen" oder "Passen" gewählt hast. Wenn du "Spielen" gewählt hast und der Durchgang belohnend ist, erhältst du die Punkte, die du zuvor gesehen hast. Zum Beispiel, wenn du in einem Durchgang die Zahl 20 gesehen hast und dich danach für "Spielen" entscheidest, erhältst du 20
Punkte. Wenn du dich für "Spielen" entschieden hast und der Durchgang nicht belohnend ist, werden dir immer 10 Punkte abgezogen, egal welche Zahl du zuvor gesehen hast.

Die Bilder, die wir dir zeigen, lassen sich in zwei Kategorien teilen: Lebendig und nicht lebendig. Beispiele für die lebendige Kategorie sind Säugetiere, Vögel und Dinosaurier. Beispiele für die nicht lebendige Kategorie sind Möbel, Kleider und Essen. Die beiden Kategorien werden unterschiedlich oft mit Punkten belohnt. Zum Beispiel: Wenn die lebendige Kategorie sehr häufig belohnend ist, ist die nicht lebendige Kategorie sehr selten belohnend. Beachte, dass das auch umgedreht sein kann und sich irgendwann im Laufe der Aufgabe verändert. Nach einer Änderung kann z.B. die zuvor sehr häufig belohnende Kategorie nur noch sehr selten belohnend sein. Die zuvor sehr selten belohnende Kategorie wäre dann sehr häufig belohnend.

Du musst herausfinden, welche der beiden Kategorien belohnender ist, damit du weißt, wann es besser ist zu spielen oder zu passen, um möglichst viele Punkte zu sammeln. Hier ist ein Beispiel für einen Spielverlauf.

Beachte, dass du in jedem Durchgang immer nur ein Bild (lebendig oder nicht lebendig) siehst. Achtung: Das ist nur ein Beispiel. Die Gewinnchancen im richtigen Spiel werden anders sein. (hier auf Gegensätzlichkeit hinweisen: zuerst ist die lebendige Kategorie häufiger belohnend (in 2 von 3

Durchgängen) und die nicht-lebendige Kategorie daher seltener belohnend (in 1 von 3 Durchgängen). Nach der Änderung ist die nicht-lebendige Kategorie häufiger belohnend (3 von 4) und die lebendige Kategorie nur noch selten belohnend (1 von 4). Immer nur 1 Bild pro Durchgang.)

Um dir dabei zu helfen herauszufinden, welche Kategorie häufiger belohnend ist, gibt es auch Durchgänge, in denen du einen anderen Spieler beobachtest. Dieser Spieler ist ein Kind, welches bereits an der Studie teilgenommen hat. Das Kind hat die gleiche Aufgabe wie du bearbeitet. Solche Durchgänge werden zu Beginn mit dem Wort "Anderer" angekündigt.

Das andere Kind hat nach den gleichen Regeln gespielt und hatte die gleichen Gewinnchancen wie du. Schaue daher aufmerksam zu, zu welcher Bilder es sah und wie es sich entschieden hat. Das Ergebnis für das andere Kind hilft dir herauszufinden, wann du am besten spielen bzw. passen solltest. Der Ablauf des Durchgangs bleibt gleich. Wenn du das andere Kind beobachtest, musst du, wenn du das Bild und die Optionen "Spielen" und "Passen" siehst die Leertaste drücken (auf entsprechende Taste verweisen). Erst dann wird dir angezeigt, wie es sich entschieden hat. Du hast 3 Sekunden Zeit, um die Taste zu drücken. Wenn du nicht rechtzeitig drückst, wird dir die Entscheidung des anderen Kindes nicht gezeigt. Du siehst dann die Nachricht "Zu langsam!". Danach beginnt der nächste Durchgang. Auch hier ist es sehr wichtig, dass du versuchst immer rechtzeitig zu antworten. Wenn du die Taste rechtzeitig drückst, wird die Wahl des Kindes in schwarz hervorgehoben. Danach siehst du das Ergebnis des Durchgangs. Dieses hat jedoch keinen Einfluss auf deine Punkte (+0), deine Punkte ändern sich also nicht. Dir werden dann die Punkte des anderen Kindes gezeigt.

Durchgänge, in denen du dran bist und Durchgänge, in denen das andere Kind dran ist, wechseln sich ab. Nutze deinen linken Zeigefinger, um die Leertaste zu drücken, wenn du das andere Kind beobachtest. Nutze den rechten Zeigefinger, um mit der rechten und linken Pfeiltaste "Spielen" und "Passen" zu wählen. Bitte lass die ganze Aufgabe über deine Finger auf den Antworttasten. Wenn du die Regeln verstanden hast, wirst du jetzt eine kurze Übung starten. Für die Übung legen wir fest, dass die lebendige Kategorie immer belohnend ist. Die nicht lebendige Kategorie ist nie belohnend. Um Punkte zu bekommen, solltest du also immer "Spielen" wählen, wenn du ein Bild der lebendigen Kategorie siehst. Damit du keine Punkte verlierst, solltest du immer "Passen", wenn du ein Bild der nicht lebendigen Kategorie siehst.

Da dies eine Übung ist, kannst du auch testen, was passiert, wenn du die jeweils andere Option wählst oder gar nicht antwortest. Probiere einfach alle Antwortmöglichkeiten aus. Die Punkte, die du in der Übung bekommst oder verlierst, zählen nicht für das richtige Spiel. Wie im richtigen Spiel sind du und der andere Spieler abwechselnd dran. Nach der Übung beginnt das richtige Spiel (1. Aufgabe).

Nach der Übung bitte nochmal darauf hinweisen, dass im richtigen Spiel die Gewinnchancen nicht 100/0 sind und neu gelernt werden müssen. Nachfragen, ob alle Regeln klar sind. Außerdem nochmal sagen, dass sich "Du" und "Anderer" Durchgänge abwechseln. Hierbei auch nochmal darauf hinweisen, dass der Ablauf beider Durchgänge gleich ist, bis auf die Antwort während der Bildpräsentation (Du -spielen/ passen mit Pfeiltasten wählen, Anderer -Leertaste drücken, um Entscheidung zu sehen) und die Änderung der Punkte (Du -Punkte des Probanden ändern sich, Anderer -Punkte des anderen Spielers ändern sich.) AUFGABENSTELLUNG 2. AUFGABE Während dieser Aufgabe wirst du Bilder sehen, immer eins nach dem anderen. Einige dieser Bilder werden die gleichen sein, die du in der Aufgabe zuvor gesehen hast. Es gibt jedoch auch neue Bilder, die du noch nicht gesehen hast. Beachte, dass du sowohl Bilder aus Durchgängen sehen wirst, wo du dran warst, als auch Bilder aus Durchgängen, wo das andere Kind dran war.

Du musst für jedes Bild angeben, ob es alt ist (wenn du es in der Aufgabe zuvor gesehen hast) oder neu ist (wenn du es noch nicht gesehen hast). Hier ist ein Beispiel für einen Durchgang: Drück die linke Pfeiltaste für die linke Option und die rechte Pfeiltaste für die rechte Option. Achte zu Beginn der Aufgabe darauf ob, "Alt" und "Neu" links oder rechts stehen. Was du auswählst, wird in schwarz hervorgehoben. Wenn du zum Beispiel diesen Wal zuvor gesehen hast, solltest du "Alt" wählen: Jedoch hast du diesen Wal noch nicht gesehen, daher solltest du "Neu" wählen: Du hast 5 Sekunden Zeit dich zu entscheiden. Wenn du dich nicht rechtzeitig entscheidest, wird dir die Nachricht "Zu langsam!" angezeigt. Danach beginnt der nächste Durchgang. Es ist sehr wichtig, dass du versuchst immer rechtzeitig zu antworten.

Wenn du geantwortet hast, sollst du angeben, wie sicher du dir bei deiner Entscheidung bist. Es gibt 4 Antwortmöglichkeiten: Drück die entsprechende Zahl auf der Computertastatur (auf Tasten verweisen). Du hast 5 Sekunden, um zu antworten.

Wähle 1, wenn du geraten hast. Wähle 2, wenn du dir unsicher oder ein bisschen sicher bist. Wähle 3, wenn du dir fast sicher bist und wähle 4, wenn du dir ganz sicher bist. Bitte nutze deinen rechten Zeigefinger, um mit der linken und rechten Pfeiltaste "Alt" und "Neu" auszuwählen. Nimm deinen linken Zeigefinger, um die Zahlen 1 bis 4 auszuwählen. Bitte lass deine Finger die ganze Aufgabe über auf den Antworttasten. Während dieser Aufgabe zeigen wir dir nicht, ob du dich richtig entschieden hast. Trotzdem werden wir dir für jede richtige Entscheidung 5 Punkte geben (+5) und für jede falsche Entscheidung 5 Punkte abziehen (-5). Am Ende der Aufgabe zeigen wir dir deinen Endpunktestand (Punkte 1. Aufgabe + Punkte 2.
Aufgabe).

Deine Angabe, wie sicher du dir deiner Entscheidung bist, hat keinen Einfluss auf deinen Punktestand. Gib also bitte eine ehrliche Antwort. If you choose PASS, you will neither gain nor lose points (+0), but we will tell you what you WOULD HAVE received if you played. This hypothetical score will be shown in brackets. The images can be divided into two categories: LIVING and NON-LIVING.

Examples of the LIVING category are mammals, insects, birds, and dinosaurs. Examples of the NON-LIVING category are furniture, electronics, clothes, and food. The two categories have OPPOSITE REWARD PROBABILITIES. For example, if you learn that the living category is rewarded 80% of the time, the non-living category will be rewarded 20% of the time.
